cells.tense: You are looking, right now, and the first clear sight has arrived without noise.
cells.ask: When something comes into focus today, stop long enough to write the exact words you'd use for it, then carry that one sentence through the rest of your day.
cells.core:
There's a way you've been looking at things lately that carries no argument in it. You see what's in front of you before you decide what it means, and you don't rush to make it useful. Most people have to work for that room; you're already standing in it.

Because the sight is clear, you also notice the thing that draws you forward — the direction you'd steer by — while it's still out of reach. You don't need it close to stay pointed at it. Here's what holds: keep that one look. Don't spend it the moment you have it. Let the pull do its work, and let the first sight stay yours while it's still new.
cells.sheetLine: You're seeing clearly, and you're following what you actually want.
cells.verb: Seeing the first clear thing before there is anything to name
cells.place: In the pull toward what you actually want, before it has a shape you could point at

cells.tense: You are looking ahead to what you'll be able to see once you finally get there.
cells.ask: Find one person who's actually in front of you today and stay with them for five minutes. No planning, no fixing, no steering. Just be where they are.
cells.core:
You're already seeing what isn't here yet — the next step, the next issue, the next version of yourself. It's not wrong to look ahead; you've got the eyes for it. But looking ahead has become the living. Real sight is happiest doing one thing at a time. It wants to land on what's here.

Instead you rush it toward what's next, and the person in front of you gets the back of your head. The direction you're drawn toward sits somewhere out there, so it gets more attention than the ground under your feet. Set the sight down once in a while and let the moment be enough. Nothing's missing that a pause won't show you.
cells.sheetLine: Everything's already in motion, and you forgot to stay put.
cells.verb: Seeing the first clear thing before there is anything to name
cells.place: In the pull toward what you actually want, before it has a shape you could point at

cells.tense: You are standing at a door that's already closed, waiting for the light to come back through it.
cells.ask: Choose one small thing you can finish today. Write the steps down, do them in order, and stop when the last one is done. Pick something under half an hour.
cells.core:
You're not looking at what's in front of you; you're watching a door that shut. The sight is there — you know the feeling of something coming clear — but it stops at the edge and goes no further. The pull toward what draws you still runs; it shows up when something good is nearby, then goes nowhere. You don't follow it, because following it doesn't feel safe.

What's starved here isn't desire. It's the act of starting, on your own say-so, without needing the light to be obvious first. Small. Completed. Yours. The direction doesn't have to be visible for you to walk a step toward it.
cells.sheetLine: The light's still there, and you've stopped walking toward it.

cells.tense: You are steering by a light you already follow, and you're telling yourself you're not.
cells.ask: Name one direction you've been moving in — one person, one project, one hope — out loud to someone who hasn't heard it. Just say where you're headed and why.
cells.core:
You've been doing this the whole time. The sight shows up, the pull arrives, and you go toward it without saying a word about it. You call it keeping options open, or doing what anyone would do. But the course has been set.

The thing drawing you isn't hidden; you just describe it as chance or mood. Because it stays unspoken, the people around you can't see what's guiding you, and neither can you from the outside. This isn't a problem to fix. It's a report to file: say the direction out loud once, to one person, in plain words. Then the choice is yours, on purpose, and the light you follow can be seen while you walk.
cells.sheetLine: You won't say it, but this light has been setting your course.

attempts.check: The draft risks claiming the person's early seeing is already producing radiance in the room — the record supports a capacity for first clarity, not proof of any effect on others. A reader could reasonably say 'it hasn't led anywhere yet,' so the core must stay with what the seeing does in them, not what it yields. The ask survives if the read is wrong: stopping and keeping one look is harmless even for someone who never had this capacity. The sentence that serves the writer is the call to own the first seeing as theirs — that can be said to anyone, so it must be reworded until it costs something to say or is dropped.
